screens.title: Deploying Azure Database for PostgreSQL and MySQL Flexible Servers
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you'll learn how to deploy and configure Azure Database Flexible Servers for PostgreSQL and MySQL. Flexible Server gives you more operational control than the older Single Server option: you can stop and start instances, choose maintenance windows, and—critically—embed the server within your Azure Virtual Network for private access. We will walk through the core decisions you must make during deployment: choosing a region and database version, selecting compute and storage profiles, integrating with a VNet and subnet for private access, and enabling zone-redundant high availability when resilience matters. You will also see concrete command-line examples for creating a VNet, a subnet, and then deploying a Flexible Server with the --vnet, --subnet, and --high-availability flags. Finally, we'll cover how to connect from a VM inside the same VNet using psql or the mysql client, and common mistakes such as underprovisioning IOPS or attempting direct public connections to a private endpoint. As you move through the lesson, notice how VNet integration and HA together protect traffic and availability for production workloads. Reflect: when would private access and zone-redundant HA be required for your applications?

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Connect, Configure, and Validate
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide focuses on post-deployment tasks and hands-on verification. You will connect to deployed Flexible Servers using common clients: psql and pgAdmin for PostgreSQL; mysql and MySQL Workbench for MySQL. If you deployed with VNet integration, practice connecting from a VM inside the same subnet or via a jump box; if you selected public access, ensure your client IP is added to the server firewall rules. Next, you will perform initial server parameter tuning such as adjusting max_connections, work_mem, and shared_buffers for PostgreSQL or innodb_buffer_pool_size for MySQL. Learn to use the Azure Portal Server parameters blade and Azure CLI to apply changes safely in a test environment first. You will also monitor resource utilization with Azure Monitor and iterate on settings as workloads become clearer. Finally, complete a validation run: confirm the server is reachable from approved network locations, run a sample workload, and observe metrics to confirm your sizing and HA behavior. These objectives guide the practical steps you need to operate Flexible Servers confidently.

screens.title: Flexible Server vs Single Server
screens.narratorSegment: Flexible Server was designed to give you operational control that Single Server lacks. At its core, Flexible Server adds features you need for production deployments: the ability to stop and start a server for maintenance workflows, set a maintenance window that fits your operating hours, and—most importantly—integrate the service into your Azure Virtual Network for private connectivity. For many enterprise applications this private access is the difference between acceptable and unacceptable security posture. Flexible Server also supports zone-redundant high availability so you can provision a standby replica in another availability zone with automatic failover. A concrete example: if you run an internal financial application that must never traverse the public internet, deploy Flexible Server into a dedicated subnet and access it only from internal VMs or VPN-connected clients. A common misconception is thinking Single Server with firewall rules equals private access; it does not. Single Server exposes a public endpoint and relies on IP allow lists, while Flexible Server can be embedded inside a VNet, removing public exposure. Takeaway: choose Flexible Server when you require private networking, predictable performance, or zone-resilient availability. When might you accept Single Server? For quick development or when private networking is unnecessary.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Flexible Server vs Single Server
Comparison: Key differences
Single Server
Public endpoint, firewall IP allow lists, limited stop/start or maintenance scheduling. Simpler to set up for quick dev work.
Flexible Server
VNet integration for private access, stop/start control, custom maintenance windows, and zone-redundant HA options for production resiliency.
Concrete Example
An internal ERP needs no public exposure. Deploy Flexible Server into a subnet and access it only from a jump box in that VNet to meet compliance and reduce attack surface.
Common Mistake
Assuming firewall rules on a public endpoint provide equivalent security to private VNet integration. They do not; public endpoints can still be exposed to misconfiguration or credential leaks.
Decision checklist
  • Do you need private, VNet-only access? Choose Flexible Server.
  • Do you need zone-resilient failover? Enable zone-redundant HA on Flexible Server.
  • Is this a short-lived dev instance? Single Server may be acceptable for speed.
Key Takeaway

Flexible Server is the production option when private networking and HA matter; do not substitute public firewall rules when privacy is required.

screens.title: Deploying a PostgreSQL Flexible Server — Core Steps
screens.narratorSegment: Deploying a PostgreSQL Flexible Server follows a small set of repeatable steps. Start by creating or selecting a resource group to hold the network and server resources. Choose a unique server name and a region that matches latency and compliance needs, and pick a PostgreSQL major version—default to the latest stable release unless your application requires a specific older version. Next, choose compute tier and size: Burstable for low traffic or development, General Purpose for balanced production workloads, and Memory Optimized for memory-heavy, in-memory operations. When you choose storage, specify the size and consider IOPS needs; underestimating storage or IOPS is a common source of future performance problems. A deployment checklist: 1) create resource group, 2) create VNet and dedicated subnet (if private access), 3) record subnet ID, 4) deploy the Flexible Server with admin credentials, sku, storage, and networking parameters. A concrete example is selecting General Purpose with 2 vCores and 128 GB storage for mid-size production workloads. Misconception check: choosing the smallest storage to save cost often forces later downtime to increase capacity—plan growth. Takeaway: plan compute and storage based on expected peak load and growth patterns.

screens.title: Compute Tiers and Storage for Flexible Server
screens.narratorSegment: Compute tiers let you align cost and performance to your workload. Burstable is designed for development or low-traffic applications where occasional C P U bursts are acceptable. General Purpose is the balanced choice for production business applications that need predictable performance without the premium of memory-optimized hardware. Memory Optimized is intended for workloads that rely heavily on in-memory operations, large buffer pools, or fast caches. When selecting storage, think about both capacity and IOPS. Storage size often determines available IOPS, and selecting too-small storage or IOPS can create a performance bottleneck under peak load. A concrete example: an e-commerce backend with frequent queries and moderate concurrency might use General Purpose with multiple vCores and 64–128 GB of storage; choose a higher storage tier if you expect heavy writes or large datasets. A common misconception is treating compute and storage as independent: they interact. When you resize storage or compute, understand the operational impact and test in a staging environment. Key takeaway: match the tier to workload characteristics and provision storage to sustain peak IOPS. Compute Tiers and Storage for Flexible Server means select compute and storage together—burstable for small, general purpose for most production, memory optimized for heavy in-memory workloads; provision iops accordingly.. In practical terms, choosing burstable, general purpose, or memory optimized and sizing storage/iops. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Compute & Storage
Compute Tier Definitions
Burstable
Cost-effective for development and low-traffic services where CPU bursts are infrequent.
General Purpose
Balanced CPU, memory, and network for most production workloads with predictable performance.
Memory Optimized
High-memory machines for in-memory operations, caching, and heavy analytics.
Storage and IOPS Guidance
Storage size impacts available IOPS. Plan for peak writes and read-heavy workloads. Underprovisioning storage often causes later performance and scaling outages.
Example
An analytics reporting service may require Memory Optimized with large storage and high IOPS, while a background job queue can use Burstable with modest storage.
Common Mistake

Choosing minimal storage to save costs, then hitting IOPS limits under real traffic. Always project growth and test under load.

screens.title: Networking and VNet Integration
screens.narratorSegment: Networking choices determine who can reach your database. Flexible Server supports two connectivity models: public access, where specific client IP addresses are allowed via firewall rules, and private access using VNet integration, which places the server inside a dedicated subnet. For production applications the recommended pattern is VNet integration because it removes public exposure and enables secure communication with other resources in the same VNet. To enable private access you create or choose a Virtual Network and a dedicated subnet, and record the subnet ID for the server deployment. You may also configure a private DNS zone such as privatelink. postgres. database. azure. com to resolve the server FQDN within the VNet. A practical connection pattern is to deploy a jump box VM into the same subnet or use a Point-to-Site VPN so developers can access the server from off-network. A common misconception is believing that adding IP addresses to the firewall will allow access to a privately deployed server; it will not. If your server is private, you must connect through the VNet. Takeaway: prefer VNet integration for production and plan your DNS and jump box strategy before deployment.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Networking & VNet
Connectivity Options
Public Access
Allow specific client IPs via server firewall rules. Simpler but exposes an internet-facing endpoint.
Private Access (VNet Integration)
Deploy the server into a dedicated subnet in a Virtual Network and use private DNS for resolution within your VNet.
Actionable Steps for Private Access
  1. Create or select a Virtual Network and a dedicated subnet.
  2. Create a private DNS zone like privatelink.postgres.database.azure.com when required.
  3. Record the subnet ID and provide it during server deployment with --vnet and --subnet flags.
  4. Use a jump box or VPN for external admin access to the VNet.
Common Mistake

Attempting to connect from a local machine to a privately deployed server without a VPN or jump box is the common cause of connection failures.

screens.title: High Availability — Zone-Redundant HA
screens.narratorSegment: Zone-redundant high availability provisions a standby replica of your Flexible Server in a different Azure Availability Zone and configures automatic failover. This means if an entire availability zone experiences an outage your standby replica can become primary with minimal manual intervention. Enabling zone-redundant HA is a deployment-time decision for most Flexible Server configurations, and it adds resilience against zone-wide failures. A concrete scenario: a retail application with a global customer base requires continuous availability during seasonal peaks. Enable zone-redundant HA to mitigate a single-zone failure during those high-traffic periods. Misconception check: HA is not a substitute for proper backups. Zone-redundant HA protects against zone outages and automates failover, but you must retain backups and a recovery plan for data corruption or accidental data loss. Also consider the cost and replication latency; zone-redundant setups incur additional compute for the standby and may have different failover characteristics than single-zone deployments. Takeaway: enable zone-redundant HA when your SLA requires automatic cross-zone failover. High Availability — Zone-Redundant HA means zone-redundant ha provides an automatically failing-over standby replica in another zone; use it when cross-zone resilience is required.. In practical terms, how zone-redundant high availability works and when to enable it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Zone-redundant HA provides an automatically failing-over standby replica in another zone; use it when cross-zone resilience is required.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Zone-Redundant HA
What is zone-redundant HA?
A standby replica is provisioned in a different availability zone and a failover is performed automatically if the primary zone becomes unavailable.
When to enable
Enable when your application SLA requires automatic recovery from a zone failure, such as e-commerce, financial, or high-availability services.
Operational notes
  • Enabling HA adds a standby replica and associated cost.
  • Failover is automatic, but you should test failover procedures in a staging environment.
  • HA is not a replacement for point-in-time backups or disaster recovery planning.
Scenario
A retail platform enables zone-redundant HA before the holiday season to ensure availability if a single data center zone has an outage.
Key Takeaway

Enable zone-redundant HA when automatic cross-zone failover is required; continue to maintain backups for data protection.

screens.title: Admin Credentials and Security Posture
screens.narratorSegment: Admin credentials are an essential part of your deployment plan. For both PostgreSQL and MySQL Flexible Servers you will specify an administrator username and a strong password during deployment. Use a naming convention that avoids common names like admin or root, and store credentials securely in a secrets store or Key Vault when automating deployments. If you deploy privately inside a VNet, register a private DNS zone such as privatelink. postgres. database. azure. com or privatelink. mysql. database. azure. com so the FQDN resolves inside your network. When using public access, add only necessary client IP addresses to the server firewall to reduce exposure. Remember the common operational pattern: for private servers, create a jump box in the VNet or configure a Point-to-Site VPN; for public servers, enforce strict firewall rules and rotate credentials regularly. A frequent mistake is assuming a private DNS or firewall change is immediate everywhere—allow time for DNS propagation and verify access from the intended client location. Takeaway: plan credentials, DNS, and access methods before deploying to avoid locked-out administrators or inadvertent exposure. Admin Credentials and Security Posture means use strong admin names and passwords, private dns for vnet deployments, jump boxes or vpns for access, and minimal firewall rules for public endpoints.. In practical terms, best practices for admin users, passwords, private dns, and firewall considerations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › CLI: PostgreSQL Deploy
Scripted Steps (annotated)
# Define variables
RESOURCE_GROUP="cohortia-pg-flex-rg"
LOCATION="eastus"
PG_SERVER_NAME="cohortiapgflex$(openssl rand -hex 4)"
PG_ADMIN_USER="pgadminuser"
PG_ADMIN_PASSWORD="YourStrongPassword123!"
VNET_NAME="cohortia-vnet"
SUBNET_NAME="pg-subnet"
PG_VERSION="14"

# Create a resource group
az group create --name $RESOURCE_GROUP --location $LOCATION

# Create a VNet and subnet
az network vnet create --resource-group $RESOURCE_GROUP --name $VNET_NAME --location $LOCATION --address-prefix 10.0.0.0/16

az network vnet subnet create --resource-group $RESOURCE_GROUP --vnet-name $VNET_NAME --name $SUBNET_NAME --address-prefix 10.0.1.0/24 --service-endpoints Microsoft.Sql

# Get the subnet ID
SUBNET_ID=$(az network vnet subnet show --resource-group $RESOURCE_GROUP --vnet-name $VNET_NAME --name $SUBNET_NAME --query id -o tsv)

# Deploy PostgreSQL Flexible Server with VNet integration
az postgres flexible-server create --resource-group $RESOURCE_GROUP --name $PG_SERVER_NAME --location $LOCATION --version $PG_VERSION --sku-name Standard_D2ds_v4 --tier GeneralPurpose --storage-size 128 --private-dns-zone "privatelink.postgres.database.azure.com" --vnet $VNET_NAME --subnet $SUBNET_ID --admin-user $PG_ADMIN_USER --admin-password $PG_ADMIN_PASSWORD --high-availability ZoneRedundant
Notes
  • Replace the example password with a securely stored secret.
  • The subnet ID is required for VNet integration; do not pass the plain name.
  • Record the server FQDN and plan a jump box or VPN for private access.
Practical Tip
Use a secure secrets store to provide admin passwords during automation and avoid embedding them in scripts.
Key Takeaway

Automate VNet and server creation, but always pass the subnet resource ID and keep credentials out of source control.

screens.title: Post-deployment: Server Parameters and Tuning
screens.narratorSegment: After deploying your Flexible Server, tune critical server parameters for workload characteristics. For PostgreSQL consider parameters like max_connections, work_mem, and shared_buffers; for MySQL the innodb_buffer_pool_size is often the most influential. The general pattern is: measure baseline metrics under a representative workload, identify bottlenecks such as high memory pressure or query planning slowdowns, and then change one parameter at a time while monitoring results. Use the Azure Portal Server parameters blade or the Azure CLI to make changes. Always test parameter changes in a non-production environment first because incorrect values can destabilize the server. A concrete example: increasing shared_buffers in PostgreSQL may improve read caching performance, but setting it too high can starve the OS of memory. A common misconception is that maximum values always yield better performance; in reality you must balance memory allocation, concurrency, and input and output characteristics. Use Azure Monitor to track C P U, memory, connections, and IOPS metrics before and after tuning. Takeaway: iterative, measured tuning reduces risk and improves performance for specific workloads. Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Server Parameters
Important Parameters
PostgreSQL
  • max_connections — limit concurrent connections.
  • work_mem — per-operation memory for sorts and joins.
  • shared_buffers — memory for caching database pages.
MySQL
  • innodb_buffer_pool_size — critical for caching InnoDB data and indexes.
Tuning Workflow
  1. Measure current metrics with Azure Monitor under representative load.
  2. Change one parameter at a time in a staging environment.
  3. Observe effects and rollback if instability occurs.
Danger
Applying aggressive parameter changes without testing can cause crashes or degraded performance.
Key Takeaway

Tune iteratively with metrics and staging tests; do not apply sweeping defaults blindly in production.

screens.title: Connecting to Flexible Servers
screens.narratorSegment: Connecting to your Flexible Server depends on your networking choice. For private access, connect from a VM that resides in the same VNet or subnet, or use a jump box or VPN. For PostgreSQL use the psql command-line client or pgAdmin; for MySQL use the mysql client or MySQL Workbench. When connecting from inside the VNet, use the server's fully qualified domain name which will resolve via the private DNS or VNet DNS settings. For public access, add your client IP to the server firewall rules and then connect to the public FQDN. A concrete example for PostgreSQL from a VM: run psql -h -U -d. If a connection fails while credentials are correct, first confirm whether the server is private and whether your client sits in the same VNet; if not, set up a VPN or jump box. A common misconception is trying to open the database to the internet by adding an IP rule for a private deployment—this will not work. Takeaway: choose the right connection path and verify DNS resolution and network placement before troubleshooting credentials. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll learn how to deploy and configure Azure Database Flexible Servers for PostgreSQL and MySQL. Flexible Server gives you more operational control than the older Single Server option: you can stop and start instances, choose maintenance windows, and—critically—embed the server within your Azure Virtual Network for private access. We will walk through the core decisions you must make during deployment: choosing a region and database version, selecting compute and storage profiles, integrating with a VNet and subnet for private access, and enabling zone-redundant high availability when resilience matters. You will also see concrete command-line examples for creating a VNet, a subnet, and then deploying a Flexible Server with the --vnet, --subnet, and --high-availability flags. Finally, we'll cover how to connect from a VM inside the same VNet using psql or the mysql client, and common mistakes such as underprovisioning IOPS or attempting direct public connections to a private endpoint. As you move through the lesson, notice how VNet integration and HA together protect traffic and availability for production workloads. Reflect: when would private access and zone-redundant HA be required for your applications?

By the end of this first objectives slide you will be able to deploy a PostgreSQL Flexible Server and configure its core runtime properties. First, you should be able to create the required Azure resource group and choose a region and a PostgreSQL version that matches your application's compatibility needs. Second, you'll learn to size compute and storage properly by selecting between Burstable, General Purpose, and Memory Optimized tiers and by specifying an appropriate storage size and expected IOPS. Third, you will configure networking: choose between public access and private access with VNet integration, create a dedicated subnet, and set up private DNS where needed. Finally, you'll enable zone-redundant high availability when your application needs resilience against availability zone failures. Each objective ties directly to common operational decisions and helps you avoid typical mistakes like underestimating storage needs. For each objective there is a short mnemonic to help you recall the configuration sequence and a verified competency milestone that you should reach when testing your deployment.

This second objectives slide focuses on post-deployment tasks and hands-on verification. You will connect to deployed Flexible Servers using common clients: psql and pgAdmin for PostgreSQL; mysql and MySQL Workbench for MySQL. If you deployed with VNet integration, practice connecting from a VM inside the same subnet or via a jump box; if you selected public access, ensure your client IP is added to the server firewall rules. Next, you will perform initial server parameter tuning such as adjusting max_connections, work_mem, and shared_buffers for PostgreSQL or innodb_buffer_pool_size for MySQL. Learn to use the Azure Portal Server parameters blade and Azure CLI to apply changes safely in a test environment first. You will also monitor resource utilization with Azure Monitor and iterate on settings as workloads become clearer. Finally, complete a validation run: confirm the server is reachable from approved network locations, run a sample workload, and observe metrics to confirm your sizing and HA behavior. These objectives guide the practical steps you need to operate Flexible Servers confidently.

Flexible Server was designed to give you operational control that Single Server lacks. At its core, Flexible Server adds features you need for production deployments: the ability to stop and start a server for maintenance workflows, set a maintenance window that fits your operating hours, and—most importantly—integrate the service into your Azure Virtual Network for private connectivity. For many enterprise applications this private access is the difference between acceptable and unacceptable security posture. Flexible Server also supports zone-redundant high availability so you can provision a standby replica in another availability zone with automatic failover. A concrete example: if you run an internal financial application that must never traverse the public internet, deploy Flexible Server into a dedicated subnet and access it only from internal VMs or VPN-connected clients. A common misconception is thinking Single Server with firewall rules equals private access; it does not. Single Server exposes a public endpoint and relies on IP allow lists, while Flexible Server can be embedded inside a VNet, removing public exposure. Takeaway: choose Flexible Server when you require private networking, predictable performance, or zone-resilient availability. When might you accept Single Server? For quick development or when private networking is unnecessary.

Deploying a PostgreSQL Flexible Server follows a small set of repeatable steps. Start by creating or selecting a resource group to hold the network and server resources. Choose a unique server name and a region that matches latency and compliance needs, and pick a PostgreSQL major version—default to the latest stable release unless your application requires a specific older version. Next, choose compute tier and size: Burstable for low traffic or development, General Purpose for balanced production workloads, and Memory Optimized for memory-heavy, in-memory operations. When you choose storage, specify the size and consider IOPS needs; underestimating storage or IOPS is a common source of future performance problems. A deployment checklist: 1) create resource group, 2) create VNet and dedicated subnet (if private access), 3) record subnet ID, 4) deploy the Flexible Server with admin credentials, sku, storage, and networking parameters. A concrete example is selecting General Purpose with 2 vCores and 128 GB storage for mid-size production workloads. Misconception check: choosing the smallest storage to save cost often forces later downtime to increase capacity—plan growth. Takeaway: plan compute and storage based on expected peak load and growth patterns.

Compute tiers let you align cost and performance to your workload. Burstable is designed for development or low-traffic applications where occasional C P U bursts are acceptable. General Purpose is the balanced choice for production business applications that need predictable performance without the premium of memory-optimized hardware. Memory Optimized is intended for workloads that rely heavily on in-memory operations, large buffer pools, or fast caches. When selecting storage, think about both capacity and IOPS. Storage size often determines available IOPS, and selecting too-small storage or IOPS can create a performance bottleneck under peak load. A concrete example: an e-commerce backend with frequent queries and moderate concurrency might use General Purpose with multiple vCores and 64–128 GB of storage; choose a higher storage tier if you expect heavy writes or large datasets. A common misconception is treating compute and storage as independent: they interact. When you resize storage or compute, understand the operational impact and test in a staging environment. Key takeaway: match the tier to workload characteristics and provision storage to sustain peak IOPS. Compute Tiers and Storage for Flexible Server means select compute and storage together—burstable for small, general purpose for most production, memory optimized for heavy in-memory workloads; provision iops accordingly.. In practical terms, choosing burstable, general purpose, or memory optimized and sizing storage/iops. Networking choices determine who can reach your database. Flexible Server supports two connectivity models: public access, where specific client IP addresses are allowed via firewall rules, and private access using VNet integration, which places the server inside a dedicated subnet. For production applications the recommended pattern is VNet integration because it removes public exposure and enables secure communication with other resources in the same VNet. To enable private access you create or choose a Virtual Network and a dedicated subnet, and record the subnet ID for the server deployment. You may also configure a private DNS zone such as privatelink. postgres. database. azure. com to resolve the server FQDN within the VNet. A practical connection pattern is to deploy a jump box VM into the same subnet or use a Point-to-Site VPN so developers can access the server from off-network. A common misconception is believing that adding IP addresses to the firewall will allow access to a privately deployed server; it will not. If your server is private, you must connect through the VNet. Takeaway: prefer VNet integration for production and plan your DNS and jump box strategy before deployment.

Zone-redundant high availability provisions a standby replica of your Flexible Server in a different Azure Availability Zone and configures automatic failover. This means if an entire availability zone experiences an outage your standby replica can become primary with minimal manual intervention. Enabling zone-redundant HA is a deployment-time decision for most Flexible Server configurations, and it adds resilience against zone-wide failures. A concrete scenario: a retail application with a global customer base requires continuous availability during seasonal peaks. Enable zone-redundant HA to mitigate a single-zone failure during those high-traffic periods. Misconception check: HA is not a substitute for proper backups. Zone-redundant HA protects against zone outages and automates failover, but you must retain backups and a recovery plan for data corruption or accidental data loss. Also consider the cost and replication latency; zone-redundant setups incur additional compute for the standby and may have different failover characteristics than single-zone deployments. Takeaway: enable zone-redundant HA when your SLA requires automatic cross-zone failover. Let's summarize the essential concepts you should remember. First, Azure Database Flexible Server for PostgreSQL and MySQL provides VNet integration, stop/start control, and maintenance window selection—features that support production deployments. Each of these concepts reduces exposure or improves predictability for production databases. As you practice deployments, keep a checklist: pick the right version, size compute and storage together, enable zone-redundant HA when your SLA requires cross-zone resilience, and validate connectivity from intended clients.
